unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to your first unit of Year 1 English. You will learn the words for things in your classroom, some colour words, and how to say your own name and how old you are. School is a happy, welcoming place, and this unit helps you feel at home in it. Say the words out loud and enjoy them — this is about brave first steps in English, not perfect spelling.
unit.learningPath:
Begin with the guided teacher launch and learn a few words through pictures and play.
Listen to the Unit story and join in with repeated language.
Complete six language, speaking, early-writing and practical activities.
If you have access to live teacher sessions, meet your teacher three times each week for two weeks for extra practice — these are optional, and every skill in this unit is also fully covered through the teacher launch, story, and speaking and writing activities above.
Finish the ten-question checkpoint, then tell an adult what you can do if one is nearby — or say it out loud to yourself.

readings.title: Amal's First Day
readings.setting: Home, online lesson or Grade 1 classroom
readings.passageScript:
Today was Amal's first day at school. She wore her new dress and held her mother's hand.

“Hello!” said a kind lady at the door. “I am your teacher. What is your name?”

“My name is Amal,” she said softly. “I am six years old.”

“Welcome, Amal!” said the teacher. “Come and see our classroom.”

Inside, Amal saw many things. There were tables and chairs. There were books and crayons. There was a big clock on the wall.

“Look!” said Amal. “A red book! And a blue pencil!”

A boy smiled at her. “Hello, my name is Adam,” he said. “Do you want to be my friend?”

“Yes!” said Amal. She was happy now.

The teacher said, “Let us sing!” All the children sang the alphabet song: “A, B, C, D…” Amal sang too.

Then the children did a treasure hunt. “Find something green!” said the teacher. Amal found a green crayon. “I can see a green crayon!” she said.

At the end of the day, Amal drew a picture of her school. She drew the tables, the chairs, and her new friend Adam.

“I like my school,” said Amal.

On the way home, her mother asked, “What did you do today?”

Amal smiled. “I learned new words. I made a friend. And I can sing the alphabet song!”

grammar.title: Name a thing in your classroom
grammar.explanation: Hold up one classroom object and name it. Say 'a' before most words, but 'an' before a vowel sound: a pen, an apple.
grammar.commonMistake: Children pop 'a' before apple by mistake. Before an a, e, i, o, u sound we say 'an': an apple, an egg. Try it slowly.
grammar.memoryTip: If the word begins with an open-mouth sound — a, e, i, o, u — use 'an'.
grammar.practice: Name three things: This is a pen. This is an apple. This is a book.

grammar.title: Describe it with one word
grammar.explanation: After naming something, tell us about it. Say 'It is' and add a colour or size word.
grammar.commonMistake: Some children say 'It big.' The word 'is' must stay in the middle: 'It is big.'
grammar.memoryTip: Point at the thing and say 'It is' first, then your describing word.
grammar.practice: Describe three school things: It is big. It is red. It is new.

grammar.title: Introduce yourself by name
grammar.explanation: Stand tall, smile, and say your own name. Use this sentence whenever you meet someone new.
grammar.commonMistake: Children sometimes answer with only their name. Say the full sentence: 'My name is...'.
grammar.memoryTip: Put your hand on your chest as you say 'My name is'.
grammar.practice: Practise three times with a friend: My name is Sami. My name is Maya. My name is Theo.

grammar.title: Say how old you are
grammar.explanation: Hold up your fingers for your age, then say the whole sentence: I am six years old.
grammar.commonMistake: Some children say 'I have six years.' In English we say 'I am six years old.'
grammar.memoryTip: Show your age on your fingers while you speak: fingers first, words after.
grammar.practice: Say your own age, then a friend's: I am six years old. I am five years old. I am seven years old.

grammar.title: Share a school skill you have
grammar.explanation: Tell your class one thing you do well at school. Begin with 'I can' and add the action.
grammar.commonMistake: 'I can to write' is a common slip. Drop the little word 'to': 'I can write.'
grammar.memoryTip: Count your skills on your fingers as you say each 'I can' sentence.
grammar.practice: Say three school skills: I can write. I can count. I can tidy up.

grammar.title: Say what you like at school
grammar.explanation: Share something you enjoy. Say 'I like' and then add the thing or the activity.
grammar.commonMistake: Children may stop after 'I like' with nothing after it. The sentence needs a thing at the end: 'I like apples.'
grammar.memoryTip: Give a thumbs up every time you say 'I like'.
grammar.practice: Say three things you enjoy: I like books. I like painting. I like break time.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this first unit, your child learns the words for things in the classroom, some colours, and how to say their own name and age. They meet the idea that school is a happy, welcoming place. The goal is warm, confident first steps in English — not perfect spelling.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is a beginner, about 5–7 years old, and is just starting to read. So YOU lead this unit — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, happy sessions of about 15–20 minutes. Lots of pointing, saying, singing, colouring and playing — very little writing.

This guide tells you what to do. The Child Activity Sheet is what your child draws and colours. The Story is one you read aloud.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with a young child
sections.body:
The grown-up holds the device and reads with the child — do not leave a 5-year-old alone with it.

Ask the tutor to say a word slowly so your child can copy the sound: “Please say the word ‘crayon’ slowly.”

Ask it to sing the alphabet song, or to play a colour-guessing game with you and your child.

Ask it to give you one more simple activity if your child wants to keep going.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching absolute beginners
sections.body:
Keep it short and playful. Stop while it is still fun.

Repeat, repeat, repeat — young children learn by hearing words many times.

Use your hands, face and voice. Point, act, and smile.

Praise every try. Confidence matters more than being correct at this stage.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Name common classroom objects (table, chair, book, pencil…).
Name and point to colours (red, blue, green, yellow…).
Say “My name is ___. I am ___ years old. I like ___.”
Say the names of some school actions (read, write, draw, sing).
Join in the alphabet song and a school poem.

sections.title: Words We Will Learn
items: Classroom objects: table · chair · whiteboard · ABC chart · clock · book · pencil · ruler · crayon · lunchbox
Colours: red · blue · green · yellow · orange · purple · black · white · pink · brown
People at school: teacher · friend · boy · girl
Action words: read · write · draw · sing · listen · point

sections.title: Songs and Rhymes
sections.body:
The “Hello, School!” poem — say it together

Hello, school! / Tables and chairs, / A list of rules, / Books and crayons. / Hello, school!

Point to each thing (a table, a chair, a book) as you say its name. Say it three times — a little louder each time!

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over several short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2–3 min)

Greet your child in English: “Hello! How are you?”

Sing the alphabet song together.

2. Learn the words (5 min)

Point to a real object (or a picture) and say the word clearly: “table”. Ask your child to repeat.

Do 4–5 words at a time. Use big smiles and lots of praise.

3. Play and sing (5 min)

Classroom Treasure Hunt: say a word (“Find something blue!”) and your child points to or fetches it.

Sing the “Hello, School!” poem, pointing to each object.

4. Story time (5 min)

Read the Story file, “Sagal's First Day”, aloud. Point to the pictures your child draws and ask the simple talk-about questions.

5. Activity sheet (5 min)

Sit with your child and do one or two activities from the Child Activity Sheet. Read each instruction aloud for them.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)

Ask: “What did we learn today?” Celebrate! Say “Well done!” and one thing they did well.

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
sections.body: Speaking comes before writing. Practise these spoken patterns often:
items: “My name is ______. I am ______ years old.”

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. Just watch and tick when your child can do these:
items: Points to and names 5 classroom objects.
Says their name and age in English.
Says one thing they can do: “I can ______.”
